title: Rise and fall of heavy cavalry
blurb: From a tame horse pulling a chariot to the salaried musketeer that retired the knight — 4000 years of military dominance, none of it planned.

steps.edge_note: The first 8000 years of domestication left horses alone. Bigger, faster, more skittish than goats — they're hard.
Once domesticated, horses go to war immediately — as a draft animal pulling a fighting platform, not as a mount.
Charioteers had control via reins braced against the yoke. Real riding needs the bit working alone.
A bridle without a saddle gets you onto the horse; both together let you stay there long enough to fight.
Once seated, the rider wants leverage. Wooden stirrups bring the foot into play — but they break.
Iron makes the same loop survive a lance impact. The Indian idea propagates west; the package finally works.
Pause on the cavalry rig. The society that will field it is being built in parallel — the agricultural revolution that pays for armor starts here.
Back to the cavalry rig. Stirrups give purchase but don't stop the rider getting punched out the back. The cantle is the missing piece.
The rig is now stable. Now it has to last — hooves wear out fast on stone roads.
Stirrups don't just stabilize — they let you transfer all of horse + rider's momentum into a point. Knights are the result.
The knight exists. Now the economy that sustains him: the collar makes the turnplow's load economical and turns Northern European clay into the breadbasket of the High Middle Ages.
Three centuries of cavalry dominance. Then the cracks: a Welsh peasant with a six-foot bow puts an arrow through plate at 200 yards.
Longbows kill from range. Pikes kill at contact — and don't need years of training. Either way the knight loses his monopoly.
Gunpowder enters the package. Pike+shot formations require neither nobility nor decades of horsemanship.
Pike-and-shot needs trained, paid, full-time soldiers. The salaried army replaces the feudal levy — and with it, the knight's role in the social order.
